domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on agent planning via MCTS and Reflective MCTS, multi-agent debate for state evaluation, and search-based agent architecture across dialogue and visual tasks. The research addresses general-purpose agent methods applicable across domains without targeting a specific application vertical. The content is primarily academic research with published results from NeurIPS, EMNLP, and ICLE venues. The talk assumes familiarity with tree search algorithms, on-policy training, and visual language models. Research-oriented presentation by a Columbia University researcher on the AI Engineer channel. Claims are supported by peer-reviewed publications and quantitative benchmark results on Visual Web Arena and OS World.

summary: Joe, a Columbia University researcher and Arklex AI founder, presents a research-oriented talk on AI agents beyond ChatGPT. He frames agents through a perception-reasoning-reflection-action loop and maps autonomy to five levels from chatbots to full-trust delegation, distinguishing low-risk back-office from high-risk customer-facing tasks. The talk addresses three themes: improving LLM reasoning, eliciting agent-optimized behaviors, and learning from traces. The first work, a NeurIPS outstanding paper, addresses self-improvement for smaller models whose noisy feedback causes error propagation ('blind leading the blind'), while large-model feedback is incompatible with smaller models' internal representations. The solution uses large models to edit smaller models' self-generated feedback, iterating until correctness, then training on-policy with filtered trajectories, reaching 48% on BIG-Bench Hard. The second theme introduces test-time scaling as an alternative to expensive pre-training. An EMNLP 2023 work applies Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to dialogue with zero training, using LLMs as policy, simulator, and evaluator; open-loop MCTS handles human response variance. GDPO achieves better donation outcomes and more natural conversations, with the model self-discovering strategies like delaying the big ask. The third area extends to visual agent tasks. An ICLE work called EXACT adapts visual language models from VQA to action-based tasks on the Visual Web Arena benchmark. EXACT introduces Reflective MCTS (R MCTS), which augments MCTS with contrastive reflection cached in a vector database for cross-task learning, and multi-agent debate for robust state evaluation. R MCTS achieves 88% on Visual Web Arena versus 16% for vanilla GPT-4V, reaches number one on the Visual Web Arena leaderboard, and is the best non-trained method on OS World. Exploratory learning further improves base models by treating tree search traversal as a single trajectory, teaching models to explore, backtrack, and evaluate rather than simply imitating best actions. Joe concludes by introducing the Arklex open-source agent framework with continuous learning and task decomposition, and outlines future work on multi-user multi-agent planning, scheduling, security, and human handover.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Agent Definition
sections.summary: Joe introduces himself (Columbia University, Arklex AI founder) and frames the talk for a research-oriented audience. He defines agents via perception, reasoning, reflection, and action, emphasizing the environment-interaction loop.

sections.title: Five Levels of Agent Autonomy and Risk
sections.summary: Using a self-driving car analogy, Joe maps agent autonomy to five levels: chatbot, agent assist, agent-as-a-service, autonomous multi-task agents, and full-trust delegation. He distinguishes low-risk back-office from high-risk customer-facing tasks.

sections.title: Talk Roadmap
sections.summary: Joe outlines three themes: improving LLM reasoning and reflection, eliciting agent-optimized behaviors from existing LLMs, and learning from traces/examples to feed back into models.

sections.title: Self-Improvement: Problem and Motivation
sections.summary: Introduces a NeurIPS outstanding paper on self-improvement. Smaller models produce noisy feedback that propagates errors, and large-model feedback is incompatible with smaller models' internal logic.

sections.title: Self-Improvement: Method and Results
sections.summary: Proposes large-model-edited feedback for smaller models, iterated until correctness, with filtered trajectories used for on-policy weighted supervised training. Three iterations reach 48% on BIG-Bench Hard, surpassing supervised training.

sections.title: Self-Improvement: Takeaways and Limitations
sections.summary: Concludes that on-policy data significantly outperforms simple SFT data, with improvement halving without it. Models can self-improve without human supervision via synthetic data. Limitation: ceiling effects when large models cannot edit feedback correctly.

sections.title: Test-Time Scaling Motivation
sections.summary: Introduces test-time scaling as an alternative to expensive pre-training. Pre-training depends on compute, data size, and parameter size, but data is limited. Test-time scaling gives models more inference steps and budgets, referencing GPT-o1 directions.

sections.title: Dialogue as Sequential Decision-Making
sections.summary: Frames dialogue tasks as sequential decision-making with lookahead planning, using a donation persuasion task as an example. Draws analogy to chess and AlphaGo-style tree search.

sections.title: MCTS for Dialogue: Method and Self-Play
sections.summary: Presents an EMNLP 2023 work applying MCTS to dialogue with zero training. LLMs act as policy, simulator, and evaluator. Uses open-loop MCTS to handle human response variance. Self-play simulated via a second LLM acting as the user.

sections.title: MCTS Results and Strategy Discovery
sections.summary: GDPO achieves better donation outcomes and is rated more convincing, natural, and coherent in human studies. The model self-discovers strategies: delaying the donation ask, diversifying persuasion tactics, and paving the way before the big ask.

sections.title: Extending to Visual Agent Tasks
sections.summary: Introduces an ICLE work called EXACT that extends planning beyond conversation to broader agent tasks involving tool use and manipulation. Motivates adapting visual language models from traditional VQA tasks to action-based tasks such as interpreting computer screenshots and performing actions like clearing shopping carts, referencing the Visual Web Arena benchmark.

sections.title: R MCTS: Reflective Monte Carlo Tree Search
sections.summary: Introduces R MCTS (RL Monte Carlo Tree Search), extending vanilla MCTS with two modifications: contrastive reflection cached in a vector database for cross-task learning, and multi-agent debate for robust state evaluation instead of single prompting. After each task, the agent reflects on successes and errors, saving experience for future retrieval. Multi-agent debate counterbalances biases by having models argue why actions are good or bad.

sections.title: R MCTS Results on Benchmarks
sections.summary: Evaluates R MCTS on Visual Web Arena (browser tasks like Reddit, shopping) and OS World (computer tasks like file system, VS Code, Excel in Linux). R MCTS outperforms breadth-first search, depth-first search, A*, vanilla MCTS, and ReAct. Achieves number one on Visual Web Arena leaderboard and best non-trained method on OS World. Augmenting visual LLMs with search improves performance without additional human supervision.

sections.title: Exploratory Learning from Search Traces
sections.summary: Introduces exploratory learning, which treats the tree search process as a single trajectory and trains the model to linearize search tree traversal, motivating it to learn how to explore, backtrack, and evaluate rather than simply imitate best actions. Exploratory learning outperforms imitation learning under constrained test-time compute budgets. Example: agent learns to try an action, evaluate undesired state, backtrack, and try alternatives.

sections.title: Arklex Framework and Future Work
sections.summary: Summarizes that Reflective MCTS relies on test-time compute scaling and exploratory learning further improves base LLMs. Announces the Arklex open-source agent framework with continuous learning and task decomposition. Outlines future work combining ML, systems, HCI, and security expertise, targeting realistic benchmarks with system integrations, multi-user multi-agent planning, scheduling, security, and human handover. Invites audience to learn more at Arklex AI.

demonstrations: Math reasoning example comparing few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought, and combined reflection prompting.
Pipeline: small model generates answer and feedback, large model edits feedback, corrected feedback updates answer, iterated until correct.
Donation persuasion dialogue task illustrating sequential decision-making and lookahead planning.
Chess tree search analogy for simulating and evaluating moves applied to conversational settings.
Computer screenshot agent task (clear shopping cart, find touchscreen coffee maker) motivating action-based visual language models.
R MCTS pipeline: builds search tree via environment interaction, uses multi-agent debate for state evaluation, caches contrastive reflections in vector database for future tasks.
Exploratory learning trajectory example: agent performs action, evaluates undesired state, backtracks, tries alternative actions.
limitations: Smaller models (e.g., LLaMA 7B) generate noisy feedback that propagates errors during self-improvement.
Large-model feedback is logically incompatible with smaller models' internal representations.
Ceiling effects occur when large models cannot edit feedback correctly, limiting smaller-model distillation.
Subjective conversational tasks are hard to train without real human interaction.
MCTS for dialogue lacks the clear, limited action space of chess, making search less structured.
On-policy data must be generated in real time because the model changes over time.
MCTS relies on expensive environment setup and interaction.
Current benchmarks evaluate single agents on single tasks, not realistic multi-user multi-agent scenarios.
quantitativeClaims: After three iterations of the self-improvement loop, 48% accuracy is reached on BIG-Bench Hard, surpassing supervised training baselines.
On-policy data significantly outperforms simple SFT data; improvement halves without on-policy training.
EXACT with R MCTS achieves 88% on Visual Web Arena versus 16% for vanilla GPT-4V without planning.
R MCTS is number one on the Visual Web Arena leaderboard and best non-trained method on OS World.
GDPO achieves better donation rates and is rated more convincing, natural, and coherent than without planning in human studies.
